title: Ezekiel 31:1–18
context: Ezekiel 31 is dated to the eleventh year, third month, first day, often placed in summer 587 BC. The LORD tells the prophet to ask Pharaoh and his multitude whom they resemble in their greatness. The answer is a parable of a great cedar in Lebanon, identified with Assyria, that grew tall by many waters, sheltered birds, animals, and nations, and surpassed every tree in the garden of God, so that the trees of Eden envied it. Because its heart was lifted up in its height, the LORD gave it to the mightiest of the nations, who cut it down; its branches fell on the mountains and its shade was abandoned. When it went down to Sheol, the place of the dead, the LORD made the deep mourn and the nations tremble, and the trees of Eden that had gone down before it were comforted. The final verse applies the parable directly: this is Pharaoh and all his multitude. Assyria’s capital Nineveh had fallen to Babylon and its allies a generation earlier, which made the warning concrete for Ezekiel’s hearers. Both traditions read the chapter as a warning against pride and as testimony to God’s rule over the rise and fall of empires (compare the tree in Daniel 4).

verses.text: In the eleventh year, in the third month, in the first day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports a word dated to the eleventh year, third month, first day. Arminians see this oracle given shortly before Jerusalem’s fall, when Egypt was still seen as a possible ally.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the date as linking the parable to the crisis of the siege. Both traditions hold the modern date loosely, often placing it in summer 587 BC.

verses.text: “Son of man, tell Pharaoh king of Egypt and his multitude: ‘Whom are you like in your greatness?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD tells the prophet to ask Pharaoh and his multitude whom they are like in their greatness. Arminian readers see a question meant to make Pharaoh reflect on his pride and on the fate of other great powers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the question as introducing a parable. Both traditions read it as inviting comparison with Assyria, which follows in the next verse.

verses.text: Behold, the Assyrian was a cedar in Lebanon with beautiful branches, and with a forest-like shade, of high stature; and its top was among the thick boughs.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says Assyria was a cedar in Lebanon, with beautiful branches, shade like a forest, and a lofty top. Arminians see Assyria pictured as a magnificent tree, a common image for a great kingdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the cedar as a symbol of power and majesty. Both traditions note that some translators read the text differently here, but the WEB names Assyria, and the parable’s point is clear.

verses.text: The waters nourished it. The deep made it to grow. Its rivers ran all around its plantation. It sent out its channels to all the trees of the field.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says waters nourished the cedar and the deep made it grow, with rivers around it and channels to other trees. Arminian readers see the sources of Assyria’s greatness, which ultimately came from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s provision behind the nation’s growth. Both traditions note that the deep and rivers may also recall the world’s waters in creation language, and they read the image poetically.

verses.text: Therefore its stature was exalted above all the trees of the field; and its boughs were multiplied. Its branches became long by reason of many waters, when it spread them out.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the cedar grew taller than all the trees, with many boughs and long branches because of abundant water. Arminians see the nation’s greatness flourishing because of the blessings it received.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing Assyria’s rise to dominance. Both traditions read the verse as setting up the contrast with the tree’s later fall.

verses.text: All the birds of the sky made their nests in its boughs. Under its branches, all the animals of the field gave birth to their young. All great nations lived under its shadow.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says birds nested in its boughs, animals bore young under its branches, and great nations lived in its shade. Arminian readers see the empire offering shelter and order to many peoples.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and compare similar images in Ezekiel 17:23 and Daniel 4:12. Both traditions see the picture of shelter as a real good that the empire later abused by its pride.

verses.text: Thus it was beautiful in its greatness, in the length of its branches; for its root was by many waters.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the cedar was beautiful in its greatness and long branches because its root was by many waters. Arminians see the tree’s beauty as a gift that depended on its source of water.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the dependence of the tree on its waters as a picture of human dependence on God. Both traditions read the verse as celebrating the cedar’s beauty before its fall.

verses.text: The cedars in the garden of God could not hide it. The cypress trees were not like its branches. The pine trees were not like its branches; nor was any tree in the garden of God like it in its beauty.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the cedars in the garden of God could not hide it, and no tree in God’s garden was like it in beauty. Arminian readers see the tree compared even to the trees of Eden, which stresses its unmatched greatness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the garden of God as a picture drawn from Eden (compare 28:13). Both traditions read the language as poetic, without building a detailed teaching about Eden from it.

verses.text: I made it beautiful by the multitude of its branches, so that all the trees of Eden, that were in the garden of God, envied it.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he made it beautiful with many branches, so that all the trees of Eden envied it. Arminians see God as the giver of the tree’s beauty, which makes its later pride a failure of gratitude.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty in giving greatness to nations. Both traditions hold that what God gives can be lost through pride, and they read the verse as a turning point in the parable.

verses.text: “Therefore thus said the Lord GOD: ‘Because he is exalted in stature, and he has set his top among the thick branches, and his heart is lifted up in his height,
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that because the cedar was lofty and its heart was lifted up in its height, judgment will follow. Arminian readers see pride as the reason for the fall, which God judges in every nation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the lifted-up heart as a rejection of God’s rule. Both traditions hold this as shared ground and compare Proverbs 16:18 by reference.

verses.text: I will deliver him into the hand of the mighty one of the nations. He will surely deal with him. I have driven him out for his wickedness.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will hand the cedar to the mighty one of the nations, who will deal with it, and he has driven it out for its wickedness. Arminians see God’s justice in bringing down a proud empire through another power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign hand in Assyria’s fall. Both traditions note that the mighty one is often identified with Babylon, which conquered Assyria, and that how God uses such powers is discussed at Judges 9:23.

verses.text: Foreigners, the tyrants of the nations, have cut him off and have left him. His branches have fallen on the mountains and in all the valleys, and his boughs are broken by all the watercourses of the land. All the peoples of the earth have gone down from his shadow and have left him.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says foreigners cut the cedar down, its branches fell on mountains and valleys, and all peoples left its shade. Arminian readers see the empire’s collapse leaving its dependents without shelter.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as describing the fall of a great power. Both traditions read the verse as a vivid picture of how quickly imperial greatness can end.

verses.text: All the birds of the sky will dwell on his ruin, and all the animals of the field will be on his branches,
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says birds and animals will dwell on its ruin and branches. Arminians see a reversal, as creatures that once sheltered under the tree now live among its fallen remains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as completing the picture of the tree’s fall. Both traditions read the verse as stressing the completeness of the empire’s humiliation.

verses.text: to the end that none of all the trees by the waters exalt themselves in their stature, and don’t set their top among the thick boughs. Their mighty ones don’t stand up on their height, even all who drink water; for they are all delivered to death, to the lower parts of the earth, among the children of men, with those who go down to the pit.’
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says this happened so that no tree by the waters will exalt itself, for all are delivered to death and the pit. Arminian readers see the purpose of the judgment as a warning to all nations against pride.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s purpose to humble human pride. Both traditions hold that all human power ends in death, and they read the verse as applying the parable’s lesson broadly.

verses.text: “The Lord GOD says: ‘In the day when he went down to Sheol, I caused a mourning. I covered the deep for him, and I restrained its rivers. The great waters were stopped. I caused Lebanon to mourn for him, and all the trees of the field fainted for him.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says that when the cedar went down to Sheol, the place of the dead, he caused mourning, restrained the deep, and made Lebanon and the trees faint. Arminians see the cosmic scale of the tree’s fall, mourned by all creation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty even over the mourning of creation. Both traditions read the language as poetic, describing the impact of a great empire’s fall.

verses.text: I made the nations to shake at the sound of his fall, when I cast him down to Sheol with those who descend into the pit. All the trees of Eden, the choice and best of Lebanon, all that drink water, were comforted in the lower parts of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says the nations shook at the sound of its fall, and the trees of Eden in the lower parts of the earth were comforted. Arminian readers see the fallen trees finding comfort that the proudest of them has joined them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the image as showing that death levels all powers. Both traditions read the lower parts of the earth as poetic language for the realm of the dead, without building a detailed map of the afterlife.

verses.text: They also went down into Sheol with him to those who are slain by the sword; yes, those who were his arm, who lived under his shadow in the middle of the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says those who were its arm and lived under its shade also went down to Sheol with it. Arminians see the empire’s allies sharing its fate, since they relied on its power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a warning to those who trust in great powers. Both traditions read it as a lesson for Judah, which had been tempted to rely on Egypt.

verses.text: “ ‘To whom are you thus like in glory and in greatness among the trees of Eden? Yet you will be brought down with the trees of Eden to the lower parts of the earth. You will lie in the middle of the uncircumcised, with those who are slain by the sword. “ ‘This is Pharaoh and all his multitude,’ says the Lord GOD.”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks Pharaoh whom he is like among the trees of Eden, then says he too will be brought down to lie among the uncircumcised and the slain: this is Pharaoh. Arminian readers see the parable applied directly, so that Pharaoh cannot miss its meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the closing words as sealing the warning. Both traditions read the comparison with Assyria as showing that Egypt’s greatness will end the same way.
